screens.title: Managing Processes
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how Linux represents running programs as processes and how to manage them with the command line. We'll define what a process is, how the kernel assigns unique identifiers and parent relationships, and how processes move through states like running, sleeping, stopped, or zombie. You will also see how to inspect processes with ps, watch them in real time with top or htop, send signals to control behavior with kill, pkill, and killall, and adjust C P U scheduling using nice and renice. These skills matter because they let you diagnose slow systems, stop runaway tasks safely, and keep services responsive. For example, if a script consumes almost all C P U, renice can lower its priority so critical services recover while you investigate. A common misconception is that killing a process with the most force is always best; instead, try a graceful termination first so programs can clean up files and flush state. By the end of this chapter you will be confident identifying PIDs, interpreting basic process output, choosing an appropriate signal, and adjusting priorities without disrupting essential services. Consider which process on your machine you would inspect first when the server feels sluggish.

screens.title: Learning Objectives (continued)
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives connect directly to everyday sysadmin tasks. When a database is slow, you will identify competing processes by PID and resource usage, then decide whether to renice, pause, or terminate the offending job. When a daemon needs a configuration reload, you will send SIGHUP rather than restarting the service, preserving uptime. When a background job hangs and creates a zombie, you will trace its PPID to find the parent and reap it or restart the parent if appropriate. You will learn safe command patterns like using ps with grep to confirm a PID before kill, and testing nice values on a non-critical process first to observe their effect. These skills reduce downtime and make troubleshooting faster and less risky. Practice will emphasize cautious, informed actions and verifying results after each change.

screens.title: What is a process? PID and PPID
screens.narratorSegment: A process is a running instance of a program that the kernel schedules on the C P U and manages in memory. Each process receives a unique Process ID, or PID, at creation. The parent process that launched it is recorded as the Parent Process ID, or PPID. This parent-child relationship matters for lifecycle: when a child exits, the parent typically waits and reads its exit status. If the parent does not reap the child, the child becomes a zombie: it has finished executing but still holds an entry in the process table until reaped. A concrete example is a shell starting a background job; the shell is the parent, and the job has the shell's PID as its PPID. A common misconception is that a zombie consumes significant C P U—zombies use almost no C P U or memory but indicate improper parent handling. When you see zombies, you should inspect the PPID to find which parent failed to reap them and either restart or fix that parent. Key takeaway: PIDs and PPIDs let you trace which processes started which, so you can stop or manage entire process groups safely.

keyIdea.title: PID & PPID
keyIdea.text: PID identifies a process; PPID links it to its parent. Zombies indicate unreaped exit statuses and usually require parent intervention.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › PID & PPID
Definition & behavior

The kernel assigns a PID when a process is created; PPID records the parent. When a child exits, the parent should reap it; otherwise the child remains as a zombie entry.

Concrete example
$ bash -c 'sleep 1 & echo $!'
1234  # PID printed by the shell
The shell starts sleep in background; it prints the child's PID. The shell remains the PPID for that sleep process.
Common misconception

Zombies are often mistaken for heavy processes. They do not use CPU; they only indicate the parent didn't collect exit status. Inspect the PPID to find the responsible parent.

Key Takeaway

Use PID and PPID to trace process trees and address zombies by restarting or reaping the parent process.

screens.title: Process states explained
screens.narratorSegment: Processes move through a small set of states that tell you what they are doing. Running means the process is actively executing on C P U. Sleeping typically means a process is waiting for input and output or an external event; it uses little C P U while idle. Stopped indicates the process has been suspended, often by a debugger or a stop signal. Zombie means the process has terminated but still has an entry in the process table because the parent has not collected its exit status. A concrete example: when a service waits for network input it appears sleeping; when you press Control-Z to suspend a foreground job it becomes stopped. Knowing these states helps you interpret listings from ps or top. A common mistake is assuming sleeping processes are harmless; while they consume little C P U, many blocked tasks can indicate slow input and output subsystems. Key takeaway: state codes are diagnostic cues — combine them with C P U and memory metrics to decide whether to investigate further. Process states explained means use state information to interpret behavior: running needs cpu, sleeping waits, stopped is suspended, zombie indicates an unreaped exit.. In practical terms, running, sleeping, stopped, and zombie — what each state means. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Process States

State summary

Quick reference to parse ps or top output.

  • R (Running) — actively executing on CPU.
  • S (Sleeping) — waiting for I/O or event; low CPU usage.
  • T (Stopped) — suspended by signal or debugger.
  • Z (Zombie) — exited but not reaped by parent.
Example: a web server worker sleeping while waiting for a request will be S, not R. A stuck loop will appear R and high CPU.
Diagnose with states
Combine state with CPU% and MEM% to decide action:
  • If R with high CPU → investigate or renice.
  • If many S processes with high I/O wait → check disk/network.
  • If Z processes exist → find PPID and address parent.
Pro tip

When zombies appear, restart or fix the parent process rather than killing the child, which is already dead.

screens.title: Using ps to capture process snapshots
screens.narratorSegment: The ps command provides a static snapshot of processes at the moment you run it. Two commonly used variants are ps aux and ps -ef. ps aux lists all processes for all users in a user-oriented format that includes USER, PID, C P U, MEM, VSZ, RES, TTY, STAT, START, TIME, and COMMAND. ps -ef offers a full-format listing that includes PPID which helps trace parent-child relationships. Use ps aux when you want to quickly find by name and inspect resource numbers; use ps -ef when you need the PPID column for hierarchy tracing. A concrete example: to find nginx processes you might run ps aux | grep nginx. A common mistake is relying solely on grep without verifying the PID — your grep itself can appear in results; prefer ps aux | grep nginx | grep -v grep or use pgrep for cleaner matching. After finding a PID, confirm the command column matches the expected process before sending signals. Key takeaway: ps is for snapshots and confirmation; combine it with grep or pgrep to locate targets safely before acting.

keyIdea.title: ps snapshots
keyIdea.text: ps aux for quick resource snapshot, ps -ef for parent/child relationships; always confirm the command before acting on a PID.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › ps
Common commands
ps aux
ps -ef
ps aux | grep nginx
pgrep -a nginx
Use pgrep with -a to avoid grepping for the grep process itself. ps output helps you copy an exact PID into a subsequent kill or renice command.
Output anatomy
  • USER — owner of the process.
  • PID / PPID — identity and parent linkage.
  • STAT — state code (R, S, Z, T).
  • %CPU / %MEM — resource shares at that snapshot.
Common mistake

Do not act on a PID before confirming the COMMAND column; PIDs recycle over time.

screens.title: ps aux vs ps -ef and using grep safely
screens.narratorSegment: ps aux and ps -ef are complementary. ps aux is user-oriented and gives a broad, readable snapshot of resource usage, while ps -ef provides a full-format view including PPID to help map process hierarchies. Use ps aux when you want to sort or scan by C P U or memory columns; use ps -ef when you need to trace parent processes or create a tree manually. When filtering, many people pipe ps to grep, but that can return the grep process itself. For example, ps aux | grep myservice may show the grep line as well. A concrete mitigation is to use pgrep -a myservice which lists matching PIDs and full command lines without the grep artifact. Another method is to filter the grep result: ps aux | grep myservice | grep -v grep. A misconception is that -ef always shows more useful metrics; it shows different columns, not necessarily more metrics. Key action: match command strings carefully and verify PIDs before signals. This avoids accidentally stopping the wrong process or a critical system component. ps aux vs ps -ef and using grep safely means ps aux for readable resource snapshots; ps -ef when you need parent information. use pgrep to avoid grep artifacts.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

ps aux

# USER  PID %CPU %MEM VSZ RSS TTY STAT START TIME COMMAND

screens.title: Signals: how processes are controlled
screens.narratorSegment: Signals are software interrupts sent to processes to request actions. The common signals you will use are SIGTERM (15), SIGKILL (9), and SIGHUP (1). SIGTERM is a polite request for a process to terminate so it can close files and release resources; it's the default sent by kill without options. SIGKILL cannot be handled or ignored; it immediately stops the process and does not allow cleanup, so use it only when SIGTERM fails. SIGHUP is commonly used to tell daemons to reload configuration without fully restarting, allowing services to pick up changes with minimal disruption. A concrete example: to gracefully stop a web server, send SIGTERM so it can flush logs; to force-stop an unresponsive worker, use SIGKILL as last resort. A misconception is to assume SIGKILL always fixes problems; while it will stop a process, it may leave temporary state or partial writes. Key takeaway: prefer SIGTERM, use SIGKILL sparingly, and use SIGHUP for reloads. In practical terms, sigterm, sigkill, and sighup — meanings and use cases. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Signals are software interrupts sent to processes to request actions. The common signals you will use are SIGTERM (15), SIGKILL (9), and SIGHUP (1). SIGKILL cannot be handled or ignored; it immediately stops the process and does not allow cleanup, so use it only when SIGTERM fails. SIGHUP is commonly used to tell daemons to reload configuration without fully restarting, allowing services to pick up changes with minimal disruption. A concrete example: to gracefully stop a web server, send SIGTERM so it can flush logs; to force-stop an unresponsive worker, use SIGKILL as last resort. A misconception is to assume SIGKILL always fixes problems; while it will stop a process, it may leave temporary state or partial writes. Key takeaway: prefer SIGTERM, use SIGKILL sparingly, and use SIGHUP for reloads. Signals: how processes are controlled means sigterm requests graceful shutdown, sigkill forces immediate stop, and sighup commonly triggers daemon reloads.. In practical terms, sigterm, sigkill, and sighup — meanings and use cases. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: kill, pkill, and killall
screens.narratorSegment: You control processes by sending signals with kill, pkill, and killall. kill targets a specific PID, so it's the safest when you have the correct identifier. pkill matches patterns in process names or full command lines and supports options like -u to target a user's processes or -f to match the full command line. killall sends signals to all processes with a given name. Use killall when you want to stop every instance of a named program, but use extreme caution because names can appear for system services you don't intend to stop. Examples

killall nginx

Use -f with pkill to match the full command line; combine with pgrep -a to test matches first.

screens.title: nice and renice: changing process priority
screens.narratorSegment: The nice value (NI) controls a process's scheduling priority, ranging from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest). A lower nice value means the scheduler will prefer that process for C P U time. Most user processes start at nice 0. Use nice to start a new process with a modified priority, for example nice -n 10 mycommand starts mycommand with lower priority. Use renice to change the priority of a running process by PID, such as renice +5 -p 12345, which increases the nice value and lowers priority. Only root may decrease the nice value below 0 to raise priority. A concrete example from practice: if a background data-crunching job is interfering with a database, start the job with nice -n 15 or renice it to a higher nice value so the database gets more C P U. A misconception is that nice eliminates C P U usage; it only shifts relative scheduling preference. Always monitor C P U and system load after adjusting priorities because misconfigured priorities can either starve important tasks or waste resources. Key takeaway: use nice and renice to balance C P U allocation safely and test changes on non-critical workloads first.

keyIdea.title: Nice & Renice
keyIdea.text: Nice sets priority at launch; renice adjusts running processes. Lower numeric values mean higher priority; root only can increase priority above default.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › nice / renice
Common commands
nice -n 15 dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/null &
renice +10 -p 34567
sudo renice -n -5 -p 12345   # requires root
Increasing nice value (positive) lowers priority. Decreasing below zero requires root and raises priority.
Practical guidance
  • Start heavy background tasks with a high nice to avoid interference.
  • Use renice when you need to change priority after observing impact in top.
  • Monitor system load after changes to verify the intended effect.
Key Takeaway

Use nice and renice to shape CPU fairness; prefer increasing nice on background jobs rather than lowering nice of critical services.

screens.title: Guided practice: monitor, control, and reprioritize
screens.narratorSegment: This guided sequence helps you practice the main commands safely. First, open two terminals. In the first run top or htop to observe system activity. In the second, start a C P U-intensive background process with dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/null &; the shell prints its PID. Next, find the process with ps aux | grep dd or pgrep -a dd to confirm the PID and command. Watch how the dd process appears in top and note its C P U%. Now attempt a graceful termination using kill. If the process refuses to stop, escalate to kill -9 but only after confirming its role. For priority practice, start another dd using nice -n 15 dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/null & and compare its C P U share in top with the default-priority job. Use renice -n 10 -p to change an existing nice value and observe the effect. Always verify with ps or top after each change. A common error is to act without confirming PIDs; the safety pattern is observe, confirm, act, and verify. End by cleaning up any background dd jobs to leave the system tidy.

In this lesson you will learn how Linux represents running programs as processes and how to manage them with the command line. We'll define what a process is, how the kernel assigns unique identifiers and parent relationships, and how processes move through states like running, sleeping, stopped, or zombie. You will also see how to inspect processes with ps, watch them in real time with top or htop, send signals to control behavior with kill, pkill, and killall, and adjust C P U scheduling using nice and renice. These skills matter because they let you diagnose slow systems, stop runaway tasks safely, and keep services responsive. For example, if a script consumes almost all C P U, renice can lower its priority so critical services recover while you investigate. A common misconception is that killing a process with the most force is always best; instead, try a graceful termination first so programs can clean up files and flush state. By the end of this chapter you will be confident identifying PIDs, interpreting basic process output, choosing an appropriate signal, and adjusting priorities without disrupting essential services. Consider which process on your machine you would inspect first when the server feels sluggish.

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to describe the lifecycle of a Linux process, interpret process listings, and control processes safely. Objective one focuses on identifiers and states: you will define PID and PPID, explain the common states a process can be in, and recognize why a zombie indicates an unreaped exit status. Objective two targets observation: you'll learn to use ps to capture snapshots and top or htop to inspect resource consumption in real time. The third objective is actionable control: you'll send signals with kill, pkill, and killall and choose the correct signal for the situation, from polite termination to forceful kill. The final objective covers scheduler tuning: you'll change nice values at launch and with renice at runtime to balance system load. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual so you remember which command to reach for—ps for snapshots, top/htop for live views, kill for signals, and nice/renice for priorities. These outcomes are practical: you'll quickly diagnose slow services, stop runaway jobs, and avoid common mistakes like overusing SIGKILL.

These objectives connect directly to everyday sysadmin tasks. When a database is slow, you will identify competing processes by PID and resource usage, then decide whether to renice, pause, or terminate the offending job. When a daemon needs a configuration reload, you will send SIGHUP rather than restarting the service, preserving uptime. When a background job hangs and creates a zombie, you will trace its PPID to find the parent and reap it or restart the parent if appropriate. You will learn safe command patterns like using ps with grep to confirm a PID before kill, and testing nice values on a non-critical process first to observe their effect. The goal is not memorizing flags but understanding trade-offs: SIGTERM allows cleanup, SIGKILL doesn't; renice can shift C P U but root privileges are required to raise priority. These skills reduce downtime and make troubleshooting faster and less risky. Practice will emphasize cautious, informed actions and verifying results after each change.

A process is a running instance of a program that the kernel schedules on the C P U and manages in memory. Each process receives a unique Process ID, or PID, at creation. The parent process that launched it is recorded as the Parent Process ID, or PPID. This parent-child relationship matters for lifecycle: when a child exits, the parent typically waits and reads its exit status. If the parent does not reap the child, the child becomes a zombie: it has finished executing but still holds an entry in the process table until reaped. A concrete example is a shell starting a background job; the shell is the parent, and the job has the shell's PID as its PPID. A common misconception is that a zombie consumes significant C P U—zombies use almost no C P U or memory but indicate improper parent handling. When you see zombies, you should inspect the PPID to find which parent failed to reap them and either restart or fix that parent. Key takeaway: PIDs and PPIDs let you trace which processes started which, so you can stop or manage entire process groups safely.

Processes move through a small set of states that tell you what they are doing. Running means the process is actively executing on C P U. Sleeping typically means a process is waiting for input and output or an external event; it uses little C P U while idle. Stopped indicates the process has been suspended, often by a debugger or a stop signal. Zombie means the process has terminated but still has an entry in the process table because the parent has not collected its exit status. A concrete example: when a service waits for network input it appears sleeping; when you press Control-Z to suspend a foreground job it becomes stopped. Knowing these states helps you interpret listings from ps or top. A common mistake is assuming sleeping processes are harmless; while they consume little C P U, many blocked tasks can indicate slow input and output subsystems. Key takeaway: state codes are diagnostic cues — combine them with C P U and memory metrics to decide whether to investigate further. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The ps command provides a static snapshot of processes at the moment you run it. Two commonly used variants are ps aux and ps -ef. ps aux lists all processes for all users in a user-oriented format that includes USER, PID, C P U, MEM, VSZ, RES, TTY, STAT, START, TIME, and COMMAND. ps -ef offers a full-format listing that includes PPID which helps trace parent-child relationships. Use ps aux when you want to quickly find by name and inspect resource numbers; use ps -ef when you need the PPID column for hierarchy tracing. A concrete example: to find nginx processes you might run ps aux | grep nginx. A common mistake is relying solely on grep without verifying the PID — your grep itself can appear in results; prefer ps aux | grep nginx | grep -v grep or use pgrep for cleaner matching. After finding a PID, confirm the command column matches the expected process before sending signals. Key takeaway: ps is for snapshots and confirmation; combine it with grep or pgrep to locate targets safely before acting.
